extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political science and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and analysis of how public opinion is formed, staged, and acts on government in the United States and England, including the social, institutional, and professional influences that shape political beliefs and tolerances. Also discusses party organization pathologies (Machine, Spoils System) and institutional reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of [corruption] the people... do not see. Venality occurs chiefly in connection with private legislation, and even in Washington very little is known about this, the rather as committees deliberate with closed doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that ordinary citizens often lack information about legislative venality; authentic knowledge is usually confined to those who have lobbied (railroad men, land speculators, manufacturers). Exception: city malversations (e.g., New York, Philadelphia) are widely known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reaction to charged accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Party newspapers accuse opponents promiscuously; supporters mostly do not believe charges they read against their candidate and tend to ignore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with a presidential contest example: supporters read their own papers which pooh-pooh charges and do not sift evidence. Notes an intermediate state between belief and disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual exposure breeds heedlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of hearing charges promiscuously bandied to and fro, but seldom probed to the bottom, makes men heedless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coupled with frequent breakdowns of prosecutions this produces lassitude rather than callousness; citizens come to accept a separate 'political morality' for politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frauds: condemnation vs proof difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Election Frauds excite strong disapproval but proof is difficult and punishment uncertain; legislative remedies have been tried and are constantly being tried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes regional exception: in the postwar Southern States manipulation to suppress negro votes was often tolerated or justified as saving 'civilization'; historical examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Machine (party organization perversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perversion by rings of the nominating machinery of primaries and conventions excites disgust proportional to fraud and trickery; the Boss is regarded as an expensive joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public often blames itself ('if we all went to the primaries...') and a feeling of fatalism exists. This disgust led to enactment of new primary laws intended to smash the Machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Spoils System and public tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation in office was seen as recognition of equality and a check on an 'aristocracy of office-holders'; favouritism seemed natural and competitive examinations pedantic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage sanctioned jobbery; ordinary citizens tolerated patronage because it was customary and not perceived as seriously wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of political vs private morality
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of politicians and the sentiment of the people differ: ordinary citizens would not in private do what many politicians do with little fear of disgrace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Europe presents a different contrast; the text emphasizes that political careers are not destroyed by acts that would ruin private reputations, and citizens judge these political vices more leniently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession-specific lenient moral codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Professions develop special codes of rules less exacting than community morals and justify deviations (e.g., 'scientific witness', Oxford degree signings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each profession tends to conceal deviations from general morality while talking of its own unsullied virtue; individual men similarly judge themselves by their surroundings and past acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: American candour vs European conventionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: America judges its own defects by past practice and gives a free course to publicity, allowing strong and frank painting of politicians' faults; Europeans interpret American frankness as cynicism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This excessive candour removes restraints that a conventional standard would impose and can lead to laxity; judged by European 'conventional' standards American politics might appear less dark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of public opinion formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion passes stages: rudimentary spontaneous impression; crystallization through newspapers and social reinforcement; debate and controversy that sharpen positions; and action (voting) which commits and solidifies opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed sequence: momentary impression at sight/hearing → confirmation/weakened by leading articles and acquaintances → evening papers more positive → debate eliminates weak arguments and cements positions → voting commits individuals and reduces multiplicity of opinion to two sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion is largely socially constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: A small part of the view which the average man entertains when he goes to vote is really of his own making; most of it is supplied by acquaintances, newspapers, and party leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments are embedded through commingling of impressions; each man believes and repeats phrases because he thinks others in his circle believe them; the element of pure personal conviction is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predispositions shape first impressions but are overlaid
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one is predisposed by previous education, habits, dogmas, affinities, and notions of self-interest which determine initial impressions, but these are soon overlaid by influences from fellows, leaders, and the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-existing habits mainly affect first impression but do not produce much independence in final opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass contribution is sentiment rather than reasoned thought
rubrics_metrics.description: For the great mass of mankind, public questions rank low among interests and they contribute sentiment grounded on a few broad considerations rather than detailed reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness and elevation of sentiment matter more than complex sifting of facts; audiences still appreciate solid arguments when presented well, but leisure and knowledge are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educated classes not necessarily more independent or accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: The educated classes are no less subject to limited independent judgment; they may be more influenced by notions of interest and timidity due to property, and sometimes closed to new evidence by conceit of competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary education, even university degrees, often do not fit a man to handle difficult political questions; less-educated may compensate with simplicity and openness of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting produces commitment and binary outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a citizen votes he is committed; after voting opinion generally becomes twofold only — a view which has triumphed and one which has been vanquished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: bringing men to the polls is like a steam roller pressing down angularities to give an appearance of smooth uniformity; after voting people back the view they sought to make prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic theory extremes caused Machine growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of human equality and popular sovereignty, when applied (e.g., electing nearly all officials for short terms), made it impossible for voters in large communities to know the fittest men, making the Machine inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains root causes: deficiency of public zeal among citizens plus excess private zeal among politicians, amplified by democratic doctrines, led to Spoils System and Machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional remedies against party Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than root out Party professionally, voters sought expedients: statutory primaries to duplicate candidate selection, limiting legislative powers and sittings, empowering strong governors, and adopting Referendum and Initiative to bypass Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reforms evolved naturally as expedients to avoid worst consequences of the Machine; primaries represent a real effort to smash the Machine and initiative/referendum aim to remove Party as a divisive force.
